title: Kidney Biopsy Aftercare: Bleeding Is the Complication to Watch
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After percutaneous kidney biopsy, focused monitoring centers on bleeding, pain, urine findings, vital signs, and ability to void. Dark-red urine, clots, worsening flank pain, dizziness, hypotension, or persistent bleeding requires prompt escalation.
recognize: Mild soreness and small transient urine discoloration may occur, but heavy hematuria, clots, worsening pain, faintness, or inability to urinate are not routine.
priorities: Monitor hemodynamics and urine, inspect the biopsy site, and report significant bleeding or worsening symptoms immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend blood pressure, pulse, pain, urine color/output, biopsy-site bleeding, dizziness, and ordered laboratory results.
interventions: Maintain ordered postprocedure positioning/activity restrictions and follow the prescribed recovery plan.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, and supplements may alter bleeding risk; medication changes must follow the procedural plan rather than independent nursing decisions.
teaching: Follow activity restrictions and seek care for heavy bleeding, fever, worsening pain, dizziness, or urinary difficulty.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be delegated; interpretation of post-biopsy bleeding and escalation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Calling new gross hematuria with clots expected because the procedure involved the kidney.
oneLinePearl: After kidney biopsy, worsening blood loss symptoms outrank routine soreness.

title: After Cystoscopy: Mild Burning Is Different From Retention or Heavy Bleeding
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Short-lived dysuria, frequency, and a small amount of blood may occur after cystoscopy, but inability to void, severe or persistent pain, heavy bleeding, clots, fever, or prolonged symptoms require clinical review.
recognize: Post-procedure irritation should improve rather than progress.
priorities: Confirm the patient can void before discharge when required and escalate retention, severe bleeding, or infection cues.
assessMonitor: Track voiding, urine color, suprapubic discomfort, fever, pain severity, and duration of symptoms.
interventions: Reinforce ordered hydration/activity instructions and postprocedure follow-up.
medicationSafety: Use prescribed analgesics/antimicrobials only as directed; do not assume all post-cystoscopy discomfort indicates infection.
teaching: Report severe bleeding, inability to urinate, fever, or symptoms lasting longer than expected.
delegationScope: Voiding/output observation may be delegated; retention and significant bleeding require licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Discharging a patient who has not voided and has increasing suprapubic discomfort.
oneLinePearl: Mild burning may be expected; inability to void is not.

title: Ureteroscopy and Stent Aftercare: Pain, Fever, and Obstruction Need Context
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After ureteroscopy or ureteral-stent placement, mild urinary discomfort can occur, but fever, escalating flank pain, persistent vomiting, inability to void, heavy bleeding, or worsening obstruction symptoms require prompt escalation.
recognize: Stent-related urgency/discomfort is different from systemic infection or obstructed infected urinary tract.
priorities: Assess pain trajectory, temperature, urine output, hydration, and infection cues.
assessMonitor: Trend voiding, hematuria, flank pain, fever, nausea/vomiting, and stent instructions.
interventions: Reinforce follow-up/removal plan and avoid pulling any retrieval string unless specifically instructed.
medicationSafety: Administer prescribed analgesic/antispasmodic/antimicrobial therapy as ordered; severe worsening symptoms should not be masked with repeated analgesia alone.
teaching: Know the stent follow-up/removal plan and urgent symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine urine observation may be shared; suspected obstruction/infection requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Assuming all flank pain after a stent is harmless stent irritation.
oneLinePearl: Stent discomfort can be expected; fever or obstructive deterioration is not.

title: After Lithotripsy: Watch for Obstruction, Infection, and Heavy Bleeding
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Passing stone fragments and some hematuria may occur after lithotripsy, but fever, inability to pass urine, uncontrolled pain, persistent vomiting, heavy bleeding, or worsening flank symptoms can signal obstruction or infection.
recognize: Stone fragments can temporarily obstruct urine flow; infection behind obstruction is high risk.
priorities: Monitor urine output and systemic symptoms and escalate suspected infected obstruction promptly.
assessMonitor: Track urine output/color, pain, fever, nausea/vomiting, hydration, and passage of fragments when instructed.
interventions: Reinforce prescribed hydration, straining, activity, and follow-up plan.
medicationSafety: Use analgesic/alpha-blocker/antimicrobial therapy only as ordered and monitor adverse effects.
teaching: Seek urgent care for fever, inability to urinate, uncontrolled pain, or worsening illness.
delegationScope: Routine urine measurement may be delegated; recognition of obstructive/infectious complications requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Treating fever plus severe flank pain as normal passage of fragments.
oneLinePearl: After stone treatment, fever plus obstruction symptoms is urgent.

title: TURP With Continuous Bladder Irrigation: Drainage Must Match the Irrigation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After transurethral prostate surgery with continuous bladder irrigation, monitor catheter patency, true urine output after subtracting irrigant, urine color, clots, bladder distention, pain, and systemic status. Sudden outflow loss with suprapubic pain can indicate obstruction.
recognize: Increasing bladder pressure/spasm, reduced outflow, large clots, or rapidly darkening drainage are concerning.
priorities: Compare irrigant infused with drainage returned, inspect tubing for kinks/dependent loops, and escalate suspected obstruction or bleeding.
assessMonitor: Trend net urine output, drainage color/clots, suprapubic findings, vital signs, and mental status/electrolytes when ordered.
interventions: Maintain prescribed irrigation and catheter traction only as specifically ordered/protocolized; manual irrigation is competency/order dependent.
medicationSafety: Antispasmodics/analgesics may help discomfort but do not substitute for checking catheter obstruction.
teaching: Avoid pulling on catheter tubing and report increasing bladder pressure/pain.
delegationScope: Measurement may be delegated; CBI adjustment/manual irrigation and complication management depend on licensed competency and policy.
examTrap: Documenting total drainage bag volume as urine output without subtracting irrigant.
oneLinePearl: With CBI, outflow must be interpreted against what went in.
sourceBasis: Contemporary TURP and continuous-bladder-irrigation nursing principles

title: Before Kidney Biopsy: Medication Reconciliation Is Bleeding Prevention
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Kidney-biopsy preparation includes identifying anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, supplements, allergies, hypertension, and sedation risks so the procedural team can make individualized hold/management decisions.
recognize: Incomplete medication lists and over-the-counter/supplement use can increase unrecognized bleeding risk.
priorities: Reconcile all medications/supplements and communicate prescribed blood thinners, NSAIDs, and uncontrolled hypertension before the procedure.
assessMonitor: Verify ordered labs, blood pressure, fasting instructions, transportation, and medication plan completion.
interventions: Reinforce the procedural team's specific medication and fasting instructions.
medicationSafety: Do not independently stop anticoagulants or antiplatelets; timing depends on indication, drug, procedure, renal function, and procedural plan.
complications: Thrombotic risk from inappropriate medication interruption
redFlags: Recent high-risk anticoagulant dose without team awareness
teaching: Bring a complete medication/supplement list and follow only the procedural team's hold instructions.
delegationScope: Medication reconciliation is licensed nursing work; prescribing/hold decisions belong to authorized clinicians.
examTrap: Telling every patient to stop all blood thinners for the same number of days.
oneLinePearl: Reconcile the bleeding risks; do not invent the hold interval.

title: After Urinary Catheter Removal: Voiding Failure Needs a Plan
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: After an indwelling urinary catheter is removed, monitor for timely voiding, bladder discomfort/distention, and residual retention risk. Do not wait for severe pain before escalating inability to void.
recognize: Small frequent voids, suprapubic pressure, overflow leakage, agitation/delirium, or absent voiding can indicate retention.
priorities: Track time and volume of voids and follow the ordered bladder-scan/retention protocol.
assessMonitor: Monitor voiding pattern, bladder discomfort/distention, fluid intake, residual volume if ordered, and risk factors such as anesthesia or urologic surgery.
interventions: Encourage normal voiding measures within plan and escalate failed void trial according to protocol.
medicationSafety: Review medications that can worsen retention, including anticholinergic and opioid effects, without independently discontinuing therapy.
teaching: Report inability to urinate, severe pressure, or frequent small voids after catheter removal.
delegationScope: Voiding measurement may be delegated; bladder-scan interpretation and recatheterization follow competency/policy.
examTrap: Assuming small dribbling voids prove the bladder is emptying adequately.
oneLinePearl: A little urine can coexist with a lot of retention.

title: Kidney Biopsy Discharge: Activity Restrictions Protect the Healing Site
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Post-biopsy discharge teaching should reinforce the procedural team's activity limits, transportation/sedation precautions, medication restart plan, and symptoms that require urgent care.
recognize: Delayed bleeding can occur after discharge, and patients may underestimate dizziness, dark-red urine, or worsening pain.
priorities: Confirm the patient can repeat the urgent warning signs and knows whom to call.
assessMonitor: Before discharge verify stable recovery findings, voiding, pain control, and comprehension of restrictions.
interventions: Provide written and verbal instructions consistent with the procedural plan.
medicationSafety: Clarify exactly when anticoagulants/antiplatelets/NSAIDs are resumed; do not give generic restart advice.
teaching: NIDDK advises avoiding strenuous activity for a period after biopsy; follow the treating team's specific restrictions.
delegationScope: Teaching reinforcement may be within PN/LVN role; initial procedural discharge plan and medication changes depend on facility scope.
examTrap: Giving only wound-care instructions and omitting delayed bleeding warning signs.
oneLinePearl: Biopsy discharge teaching is mostly about delayed bleeding recognition and safe activity.

title: After Urologic Instrumentation: Fever Is Not Just Procedure Irritation
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Mild urinary irritation can follow cystoscopy or ureteroscopy, but fever, rigors, worsening flank pain, hypotension, or systemic illness after urinary instrumentation can indicate infection and requires prompt evaluation.
recognize: New fever plus urinary/flank symptoms is more concerning than isolated brief dysuria.
priorities: Assess vital signs, urine output, pain location, mental status, and sepsis cues and escalate promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, BP/HR, urine findings, voiding, flank/suprapubic pain, and ordered cultures/labs.
interventions: Obtain ordered specimens before antibiotics when feasible without delaying urgent therapy in unstable infection.
medicationSafety: Do not start leftover antibiotics or assume prophylaxis prevents postprocedure infection.
teaching: Seek care for fever, chills, severe pain, or inability to void after urinary instrumentation.
delegationScope: Routine vitals/output may be delegated; sepsis recognition and escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Reassuring a febrile patient that burning is expected after cystoscopy.
oneLinePearl: Irritation can be expected; systemic infection signs are not.
sourceBasis: NIDDK Cystoscopy and Ureteroscopy aftercare guidance

title: Gross Hematuria With Clots: Protect Urine Outflow and Circulation
bottomLine: After a urinary procedure, gross hematuria with clots can obstruct outflow and may represent significant bleeding. Increasing suprapubic pain, reduced drainage, large clots, dizziness, or hemodynamic change requires urgent escalation.
recognize: Bladder distention with decreasing catheter output despite ongoing bleeding suggests clot retention rather than improvement.
priorities: Assess catheter/voiding patency, bleeding severity, bladder distention, and hemodynamics; notify the urologic team promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend urine color/volume/clots, pain, bladder findings, pulse/BP, and ordered hemoglobin.
interventions: Maintain ordered catheter/irrigation system; manual irrigation or catheter replacement requires specific competency/order.
medicationSafety: Communicate anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy and do not independently reverse or hold unless authorized.
teaching: Report bright-red urine, clots, inability to urinate, or increasing pressure promptly.
delegationScope: Urine observation may be delegated; clot-retention troubleshooting and invasive interventions are competency/policy dependent.
examTrap: Interpreting less catheter drainage as bleeding resolution without checking for obstruction.
oneLinePearl: Less output during heavy hematuria may mean a clot has blocked the way out.
